OLAYLAR:1453-05-29:0.d: After a siege of fifty-four days (6 April–29 May 1453), on the morning of 29 May the Ottoman army crossed the walls and entered the city; the last emperor, Constantine XI, died in the fighting and the 1,100-year-old Eastern Roman Empire passed into history. The young sultan took the title 'the Conqueror' (Fatih), made the city his capital and converted Hagia Sophia into a mosque; the city was soon revived by resettlement and construction. According to the TDV, Silivri and Vize were definitively conquered only in 1453; according to the TDV entry on Lemnos, the island came under Ottoman administration immediately after the conquest and was left to the Gattilusio family on condition of tribute. The casting of giant cannon, the overland transport of ships and the siege arrangement before the walls are regarded as the peak of the military engineering of the period. In European historiography the conquest is counted among the symbolic dates of the end of the Middle Ages.

OLAYLAR:1699-01-26:0.d: By Karlowitz, which ended the sixteen years of Holy League wars, Hungary and Transylvania were left to Austria, Podolia to Poland, and the Morea and the Dalmatian coasts to Venice. For the first time in Ottoman history territory on this scale was being lost at the negotiating table and permanently; the treaty is regarded as the opening document of the new era in which the empire went on the defensive against Europe, and is also a turning point in Ottoman diplomatic history. Settlements that changed hands on the same day: Kostajnica and Jasenovac (from the Ottomans to the Habsburgs; the text of the treaty leaves Castanoviz in the emperor's hands, the surrender day of Jasenovac is not in the source, the treaty day was taken as the basis) and Preveza (from Venice to the Ottomans; TDV Karlofça: under the provision signed on 24 Rajab 1110 / 26 January 1699, Venice's occupied places north of the Gulf of Lepanto were returned). The map also shows Kostajnica and Jasenovac on the Habsburg side, Uman and Vinnytsia in Right-Bank Ukraine as having passed from the Ottomans to Poland (TDV Merzifonlu Kara Mustafa Paşa; IEU Vinnytsia: Turkish rule 1672-99) and Nadin in Dalmatia as belonging to Venice (no settlement-specific surrender day in the source, the treaty day was taken as the basis; the start and end dates of Nadin's period were not verified against a source — approximate information). Vonitsa, north of the Gulf of Lepanto, is also returned from Venice to the Ottomans (TDV Karlofça); in Dalmatia Vrana (Urana) is among the places remaining with Venice (period date not verified — approximate information).

OLAYLAR:1739-09-18:0.d: At the end of the war (1736–1739) conducted on two fronts against Austria and Russia, Belgrade and Northern Serbia were recovered; Russia agreed to demilitarize Azov and not to keep a fleet on the Black Sea. The treaty, regarded as the last great success of 18th-century Ottoman diplomacy and army, gave the empire a quarter-century period of peace. Other settlements returning from Austria to the Ottomans on the same day: Hisarcık (Grocka) (the date of Belgrade was taken as the basis; TDV Belgrad), Craiova, Râmnicu Vâlcea and Turnu Severin (the return of Lesser Wallachia to the Ottomans, to Wallachian vassalage). Bosanski Brod and Bosanska Dubica on the Sava strip, however, return to the Ottomans on the map on 28 September 1739 (TDV Bosna-Hersek; TDV I. Mahmud: 28 September 1739). Târgu Jiu in Lesser Wallachia also returns to the Ottomans on the same day.

OLAYLAR_EK:1324-01-01:0.d: Akyazı became a target of Ottoman raids in the time of Osman Bey (in the years after the 1305 campaign); the exact year of its capture is unknown. No source gives when the Island of İmralı was taken. The 1324 boundary on the map is an approximate placeholder.

OLAYLAR_EK:1328-01-01:0.d: After the capture of Kandıra, Akça Koca, together with Konuralp and Gazi Abdurrahman, took the fortress of Aydos near Kartal, and then the fort of Samandıra to its north; the region of Samandıra was given to him as property. Akça Koca died near Kandıra in 1328; the region where he had served as frontier lord was given to Prince Murad.

OLAYLAR_EK:1334-01-01:0.d: The coastal town of Gemlik (Kios) on the Gulf of Gemlik, which opens onto the Marmara, passed into Ottoman hands. When Bursa surrendered in 1326, the city's tekfur had been sent to Gemlik with his family; that is, Gemlik was still in Byzantine hands in 1326. No separate date was found for Armutlu; on the map the date of Gemlik has been taken as the basis for it.

OLAYLAR_EK:1461-06-01:0.d: The Candaroğlu ruler of Sinop surrendered without a fight; the way was opened for the Trebizond campaign. Other places annexed on the same date: Kastamonu, Bartın, Safranbolu. The TDV entry on the Candaroğlus also mentions Bolu, Eflani and Tosya among the lands of the Candaroğlu beylik annexed in 1461; on the map these three places, too, pass on this day from Candaroğlu to the Ottomans. Other settlements lost on the same date: Karadeniz Ereğli, Devrek, Akçakoca (Candaroğlu land).

OLAYLAR_EK:1526-09-01:0.d: As the Ottoman army marched on Buda after the victory of Mohács, the keys of the city were presented to the sultan on 11 September 1526; however, the Lawgiver did not hold Buda and withdrew his army. In Hungary, left without a king, the nobles elected two separate kings: János Szapolyai on 10 November 1526, and the Habsburg Ferdinand I on 17 December 1526. Ferdinand took Buda in August 1527. Szapolyai's settling in Buda as a king under Ottoman protection would come with the campaign of 1529 (see the 1529 entry), and direct Ottoman administration would be established in 1541.

OLAYLAR_EK:1717-08-18:0.d: After the rout at Petrovaradin and the loss of Temesvár, Prince Eugene besieged Belgrade; when the relief army that came to save the city was also routed, the fortress surrendered. The city, which had been retaken in 1690 after Karlowitz, was thus lost again and the Danube line of defense collapsed. Belgrade could be recovered only twenty-two years later, by the 1739 Treaty of Belgrade. Other settlements lost on the same date: Smederevo. The map also shows the areas of Hisarcık (Grocka) and Yagodina (Jagodina) as belonging to the Habsburgs on this day (the day given for the region; the day at place level is not in the source, approximate information); Mehadia, however, passes to the Habsburgs on 27 August 1717 (Bánlaky 0019/1715).

OLAYLAR_EK:1395-06-03:0.d: After the raid at Rovine, Bayezid the Thunderbolt took Nicopolis; the Bulgarian tsar Ivan Shishman, who sat there as an Ottoman vassal, was eliminated.

OLAYLAR_EK:1478-01-15:0.d: Grand Prince Ivan III removed the symbolic bell of the popular assembly (veche) in Novgorod, replaced the local officials with his own governors and in effect bound the city to Moscow; Novgorod ceased to be an independent republic. The land of Novgorod stretched from the Baltic Sea to the White Sea and the Urals.

OLAYLAR_EK3:1688-09-06:0.d: Belgrade, which had been in Ottoman hands since 1521, surrendered to the Holy League army; the gates of Serbia were opened to the enemy and the danger reached the Niš-Sofia line. Another settlement passing from the Ottomans to the Habsburgs on the same day: Hisarcık (Grocka) — the date of Belgrade was taken as the basis (TDV Belgrad; approximate information).

OLAYLAR_EK3:1689-08-01:0.d: Margrave Ludwig von Baden crossed the Morava at Pasarofça in August 1689 and advanced toward Niš; the town remained in Austrian hands until the summer of 1690 (TDV II. Süleyman says that Pasarofça was retaken in 1690). The day and the information taken from Röder have not been re-verified.

OLAYLAR_EK3:1689-10-25:0.d: After the bloodless taking of Vidin (October 1689, TDV Vidin), Baden repaired and garrisoned Orsova and Fethülislâm on 25 October 1689; Orsova remained Austrian until the autumn of 1690. The day rests on Bánlaky/Röder and has not been re-verified.

OLAYLAR_EK3:1690-09-27:0.d: Fazıl Mustafa Pasha set out on campaign in July 1690; after Şehirköy (Pirot), Passarowitz and Güvercinlik (Golubac) were taken, Niš, which was besieged, fell into Ottoman hands on 27 September 1690 (TDV Semendire). At the same time Vidin had also been retaken. Other settlements returning from the Habsburgs to the Ottomans on the same day: Jagodina and Ürküp (Prokuplje) — the Niš day was taken because no day at place level could be found (TDV Semendire; approximate information; Röder (1842), however, writes that the vizier passed through Jagodina on 8-24 September; this contradiction could not be resolved).

OLAYLAR_EK3:1690-10-08:0.d: The grand vizier Köprülüzade Fazıl Mustafa Pasha retook Belgrade from Austria on 8 October 1690; the city lost in 1688 thus returned to the Ottomans (TDV II. Süleyman). Another settlement returning from the Habsburgs to the Ottomans on the same day: Hisarcık (Grocka) — the date of Belgrade was taken as the basis (TDV II. Süleyman; approximate information).

OLAYLAR_EK3:1695-09-22:0.d: On the first campaign in which the sultan personally took part, Lipova was retaken and Austrian forces were defeated at Lugoj; the first break occurred in the chain of defeats that had lasted for years. The map also shows Caransebeș as having returned from the Habsburgs to the Ottomans in this campaign; the source gives only September 1695 (TDV II. Mustafa), the day was taken from that of Lugoj (approximate information).

OLAYLAR_EK4:1815-01-20:0.d: The Saudis, who suffered a heavy defeat in the pitched battle, withdrew to the interior. The truce that was made did not last; two years later the operation would be carried into the heart of Najd. After this victory Turaba and Hurma east of Ta'if are shown on the map as having left Saudi hands (event source Lorimer, Gazetteer; the settlement-specific attestation and the 13 January day are approximate information).

OLAYLAR_EK4:1832-07-29:0.d: The defensive line was broken in the narrow pass in the Amanus mountains. Antioch, Adana and Tarsus passed to the Egyptian forces (the occupation of Maraş, according to TDV, is 1833); on the map Çukurova is shown in the tone of dependent territory. The road into the interior of Anatolia was now undefended.

OLAYLAR_EK4:1832-09-13:0.d: The Gülek Pass, the Çukurova gate of the Taurus, fell into the hands of the Egyptian army. Ibrahim Pasha appointed his own mütesellim to the Sancak of İçil, and all the landing places on the coast came under Egyptian control. On the map Mersin and Silifke are shown as attached to Egypt from this day (the day of the appointment is not in the source; this date is a lower bound); since in the Kütahya decision only the muhassıllık of Adana was transferred, this control ends with the evacuation of Anatolia.

OLAYLAR_EK4:1833-01-01:1.d: Karahisâr-ı Sâhib, on the route of the Egyptian army advancing to Kütahya after the Battle of Konya, remained for a time in the hands of Ibrahim Pasha in 1833. On the map the city is the source-based intermediate point of the occupation line between Konya and Kütahya; no city-level testimony could be found for Akşehir, Ilgın and İshaklı, and these places are shown in the Ottoman colour.

OLAYLAR_EK5:1514-09-06:0.d: Following the victory at Chaldiran, the Ottoman army entered the Safavid capital Tabriz, and the khutba was read in the city in the name of the sultan. Selim stayed there for a week and had some of the artists and scholars (ulema) of Tabriz transferred to Istanbul; this transfer was to have a profound influence on Ottoman court art. Although the city was abandoned as winter approached and because of the discontent of the Janissaries, Safavid superiority in the East had been broken. The places that passed to the Ottomans on the map on this day are not contiguous with one another: Tabriz is a nine-day army occupation; the plain of Erzincan surrendered without a fight during the campaign, while the fortress of Kemah in its midst held out as Safavid until 19 May 1515; Siirt was recovered from the Safavids by Halil Bey, the ruler (melik) of Hasankeyf, who had been freed from Shah Ismail's imprisonment in Tabriz and submitted to the Ottomans — Diyarbakır around it remained Safavid until 1515, and Hasankeyf until 1517.

OLAYLAR_EK5:1518-01-01:0.d: Although Ottoman influence in the region grew after the victory at Chaldiran (1514), the full seizure of Erzurum was delayed until Iranian influence was broken; the city came under Ottoman administration only in 1518-19, after the Egyptian campaign. Erzurum had come under Safavid rule in 1502, when Shah Ismail ended the Aqquyunlu Principality; that sixteen-year period was thus closed. In 1534, during the Campaign of the Two Iraqs, the Erzurum beylerbeylik would be established. Between 1518 and 1519, Aşkale, together with the Erzurum region, came under Ottoman administration (its day could not be verified).

OLAYLAR_EK5:1716-10-13:0.d: After the Varadin rout, Prince Eugène marched directly on Temesvár, and after a siege of more than forty days the fortress was surrendered by capitulation. The city, conquered in the time of Süleyman the Lawgiver in 1552 and regarded for 164 years, as a beylerbeylik center, as the eastern pillar of the defense of Hungary, was thus lost. With the fall of Temesvár the whole of the Banat region passed to Austria and the Ottoman frontier was pushed south of the Danube. Other settlements passing from the Ottomans to the Habsburgs on the same day: Csákóvár, Facset and Caransebeș — together with the transfer of the Temesvár eyalet (TDV Timişvar; no day at place level in the source, the date of the center to which they were attached was taken as the basis; approximate information).

OLAYLAR_EK5:1716-11-16:0.d: After the fall of Temesvár, the Austrian cavalry general Mercy, charged with taking the rest of the Banat, marched on 14 November on Haram (Yeni Palanka) on the Danube bank; when he reached the fortress on 16 November, the 200-man Ottoman garrison raised a white flag and surrendered on condition of free withdrawal. Thus the Danube line of Southern Banat, in Ottoman hands since 1552, also passed to Austria. Another settlement passing from the Ottomans to the Habsburgs on the same day: Vršac — the date of Haram was taken as the basis (Bánlaky 0019/1703; approximate information).

OLAYLAR_EK5:1732-01-08:0.d: After Nadir Shah's victory at Malayer and successive Iranian offensives, the governor of Baghdad Ahmed Pasha signed a peace text without consulting the center. According to the treaty the Aras river was accepted as the border; Western Iranian cities such as Hamadan, Kermanshah, Ardalan, Ardabil and Tabriz were returned to Iran, while Ganja and Tbilisi remained Ottoman. This text, which was received with reaction in Istanbul, was found insufficient by Nadir Shah as well, and before the year 1732 was out the war flared up again. The map also shows Kotur, which is considered to have shared the same fate as Hoy, as having passed from the Ottomans to the Safavids on this day (TDV Hoy; no day specific to Kotur in the source — approximate information).

OLAYLAR_EK5:1775-05-07:0.d: Exploiting the weakness caused by Küçük Kaynarca, Austria demanded Bukovina, the region linking Moldavia and Transylvania, and obtained this land without going to war, through threats and bribery. The loss of this fertile and strategic region southwest of Khotin effectively split the voivodeship of Moldavia in two. This cession, made without a single shot being fired, was regarded as one of the clearest signs that the Ottoman State had lost its deterrent power. With the cession of Bukovina in 1775, Suceava and Czernowitz passed to Austria (its day could not be verified).

OLAYLAR_EK5:1791-08-04:0.d: Thanks to Prussian pressure and the Austrian preoccupation with the French Revolution in the west, the two states reached peace on the basis of the pre-war borders. Austria gave back all the places it had occupied, including Belgrade; the Ottoman State accepted only small corrections on the Croatian frontier. The closing of the western front on these terms enabled the Ottoman State to concentrate all its strength against Russia and limited the loss in the Treaty of Iași. With these corrections on the Croatian frontier Cetin (Cetingrad) and Drežnik Grad pass from the Ottomans to the Habsburgs (TDV Ziştovi Antlaşması; Korić 2016, n. 118, article 4). Orsova (Old Orsova), however, is the only place not returned (Bánlaky 0019/1796); on the map this day is taken as the basis for the legal transfer (de facto occupation 16 April 1790).

OLAYLAR_EK5:1875-06-19:0.d: The uprising of Christian peasants around Nevesinje because of heavy taxes and the pressure of the ayans spread within a short time to the whole of Herzegovina and was fed by volunteers coming from Serbia and Montenegro. The rebellion, which led to reform impositions by Austria and Russia, triggered the Bulgarian uprisings and the Serbian-Montenegrin declarations of war the following year. Thus the first link was formed in the great chain leading to the '93 War and, by the Treaty of Berlin, to the loss of the Balkans.

OLAYLAR_EK5:1900-09-01:0.d: Construction of the line, ordered by the irade of Abdülhamid II dated 2 May 1900, began on 1 September 1900 with an official ceremony held at Damascus. The project, built entirely with donations collected from the Islamic world and the labour of Ottoman engineer-soldiers, reduced the pilgrims' journey from Damascus to Medina from forty days to five. It was both a work of prestige reinforcing the spiritual authority of the caliphate and a strategic investment strengthening military control over the Hijaz.

OLAYLAR_EK5:1715-07-20:0.d: Nauplia, the Venetian capital in the Morea and its strongest fortification, fell with the capture of the Palamidi bastion after a nine-day bombardment. The fortress's being taken so quickly broke resistance in the rest of the peninsula. The recovery of the Morea, lost at Karlowitz, was effectively completed here. Another settlement passing from Venice to the Ottomans on the same day: Argos — the date of Nauplia was taken as the basis (TDV Anabolu; approximate information).

OLAYLAR_EK5:1718-07-21:0.d: The Morea had been retaken from Venice, but Austria, which entered the war, prevailed at the table with the victories it won at Petrovaradin and Belgrade. The treaty signed through the mediation of England and the Netherlands left the Morea with the Ottomans, while in return Northern Serbia together with Belgrade, the Banat and Lesser Wallachia were left to Austria; in the TDV's words 'Northern Bosnia was entirely left to Austria' — fortresses such as Bosanska Dubica and Bosanski Brod along the Sava pass to Austria on the map from this day (the exact border was drawn one by one by commissioners, the TDV does not name these fortresses); Venice, however, kept its positions on the Ionian coast such as Preveza and Kythira. By the trade capitulation signed on the same day the customs duty taken on Austrian goods was reduced from five percent to three. While the treaty registered the Ottoman State's retreat in Central Europe, the twenty-seven-year peace it opened laid the ground of the Tulip Era (1718-1730): the first Ottoman printing press (1727, İbrahim Müteferrika), translation committees, smallpox inoculation observations and a new palace-cultural life under Nevşehirli Damad İbrahim Pasha were products of these years of peace. Other settlements that changed hands on the same day: Craiova, Râmnicu Vâlcea and Turnu Severin (Lesser Wallachia/Oltenia, from the Ottomans to Austria) and Ayamavra (Lefkada) (from the Ottomans to Venice; TDV Ayamavra: in 1718 by the Treaty of Passarowitz the island was left to Venice). In Lesser Wallachia Târgu Jiu also passes to Austria; Vonitsa (TDV Pasarofça Antlaşması) and Kythira (TDV Çuka Adası: article 3 of Passarowitz) pass to Venice.

OLAYLAR_EK5:1798-10-23:0.d: When the Republic of Venice was destroyed in 1797, the Ionian islands and the mainland Preveza, Parga and Vonitsa fell into French hands. Ali Pasha of Tepelena, governor of Ioannina, exploiting the war opened by the French invasion of Egypt, marched on Preveza and inflicted a heavy defeat on the French garrison at the ruins of Nicopolis outside the city. Thus this port, left to Venice at Passarowitz, came under Ottoman administration eighty years later. Butrint fell on 25 October when the French garrison blew up the fortifications and withdrew to Corfu (Curlin, Preveza B, 2010; the date of Preveza is taken as the basis on the map) and came under Ottoman administration.

OLAYLAR_EK5:1688-06-22:0.d: After Antonio Caraffa's three-day siege, Lipova surrendered between 12 and 22 June 1688 and passed into Austrian hands. The Ottomans later retook the city, Austria recaptured it in 1691; in the campaign of 1695 the Ottomans regained control. Other settlements that passed from the Ottomans to the Habsburgs on the same date: Arad and Világos (Şiria). For Arad the source gives only the year (MKL, Arad: in Ottoman hands between 1551 and 1688); the day is taken from Lipova, and for Világos the date of Arad was taken as the basis (approximate information). The fortresses of Lugos (Lugoj) and Karánsebes (Caransebeş) also passed to Austria at the end of June (Bánlaky 0016/1302 'Jenővel elveszett Lugos és Karánsebes'; 0017/1443 'június végén').

OLAYLAR_EK5:1387-01-22:0.d: Muş, which had passed to Qaraqoyunlu rule after the Mongol period, came under the administration of Timur, who held Qaraqoyunlu lands, in 789 (1387).

OLAYLAR_EK6:1730-08-12:0.d: The Western Iranian cities taken in 1723-1727 by exploiting the collapse of the Safavid State were lost one by one to the offensive of Nadir Khan, who seized actual power in Iran. In Azerbaijan Ardabil and Khalkhal also fell into Nadir's hands. The loss of Hamadan, Kermanshah and Qasr-i Shirin had a heavy echo in Istanbul; the army's not setting out on campaign but waiting at Üsküdar and the attempt to cover up the loss were among the direct causes of the Patrona Halil Revolt that broke out six weeks later. The map also shows Kotur, which is considered to have shared the same fate as Hoy, as having passed from the Ottomans to the Safavids on this day (Uluerler 2015, Turkish Studies 10/5, p. 6; no day specific to Kotur in the source — approximate information).

OLAYLAR_EK6:1547-01-01:0.d: The sancak of Bayezid, in the middle of the Ottoman-Safavid frontier, passed again into Iranian hands (Kaya 2017 mentions this 'together with Van and Erciş'; however, according to Karataş 2025 and the TDV, Van and Erciş had returned to the Safavids on 22 September 1535); in this change of hands some places in the sancak were ruined. The sancak changed hands between the two states many times until the last quarter of the 16th century.

OLAYLAR_EK6:1686-10-23:0.d: Szeged, at the confluence of the Tisza and Maros rivers, was the southern gate of the Hungarian plain and held the road to the Temesvár eyalet. After Buda and Pécs fell in the same autumn, the besieged fortress surrendered quickly. The loss of three fortresses in one season was a sign that the Ottoman administrative structure in Hungary, established since 1541, had begun to collapse. The map also shows Zenta on the Tisza as having passed from the Ottoman to the Habsburg side on the same day (the surrender day specific to Zenta could not be verified from the source, the day was taken from Szeged; TDV Zenta: from October 1686 fighting began between the Ottomans and the allies led by the Habsburgs — approximate information).

OLAYLAR_EK6:1689-02-03:0.d: Szigetvár was the fortress where Süleyman the Lawgiver died during the siege in 1566 on his thirteenth and last campaign; for this reason it had a symbolic place in Ottoman memory. A hundred and twenty-three years later, after all the fortresses around it had fallen, the fortress, protected by marshes, surrendered too. The mausoleum where the Lawgiver's internal organs were buried and the town around it were destroyed after it passed to Habsburg rule. Another settlement passing from the Ottomans to the Habsburgs on the same day: Barcs — the date of Szigetvár was taken as the basis (Bánlaky 0017/1449; approximate information).

OLAYLAR_EK6:1833-04-12:0.d: Athens, Ottoman since 1456, had changed hands several times during the Greek war of independence, and the garrison on the Acropolis had returned to Ottoman control in 1827. Because it lay north of the border drawn by the London Protocol, the city was handed over to the new kingdom and the garrison evacuated the Acropolis. The day taken as the basis on the map is the day the Bavarian troops took over the Acropolis; the actual departure of the Ottoman garrison took place a few days later (St Clair, Who Saved the Parthenon?, Open Book Publishers, 2022, ch. 13; Finlay, Journals and Letters, vol. I, p. 67). The following year Athens was declared the capital of Greece in place of Nauplia.

OLAYLAR_ILIRYA0072:1806-02-01:0.d: The Treaty of Pressburg (Bratislava/Pressburg) of 26 December 1805 forced Austria to give up Istria, Dalmatia and all the Adriatic islands. France effectively took over the administration in February 1806; Zadar remained the seat of the governor-general (proveditor), and between 1806 and 1810 this office was held by the Venetian Vincenzo Dandolo. Dalmatia was added to the Illyrian Provinces after the 1809 Treaty of Schönbrunn. The first Austrian administration, which had lasted since 1797, thus came to an end.

OLAYLAR_ILIRYA0072:1806-01-01:0.d: After the Treaty of Pressburg, the Kvarner islands — unlike Dalmatia — were attached not directly to France but to Napoleon's Kingdom of Italy; they entered the Illyrian Provinces only in 1809. In the Bay of Kotor, Austrian administration ended and Russian administration was established between 1806 and 1807; the Bay passed to France only in 1807.

OLAYLAR_ILIRYA0072:1779-01-01:0.d: When the forces of the First Saudi State seized the emirate of Ha'il, the administration of the city was in the hands of the Ibn Ali family of the Abde clan of the Shammar tribe. This family ruled Ha'il until 1835, when Abdullah b. Rashid seized the emirate; the Rashidid dynasty was founded only at that date. The source names the emir of the city in 1820.

OLAYLAR_EK7:1920-04-23:0.d: After the dissolution of the Chamber of Deputies in Istanbul, the deputies assembled in Ankara and opened the Grand National Assembly of Turkey, and Mustafa Kemal Pasha was elected chairman of the assembly. According to the TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi entry on the Grand National Assembly of Turkey, the assembly had an extraordinary character, concentrating both legislative and executive authority in itself. This opening was the turning point at which the political and institutional center of the national struggle moved to Ankara. On the map, with this event 124 settlements (the unoccupied regions of Turkey), including Konya, Sivas, Kayseri, Eskişehir, Erzurum, Trabzon, Samsun, Diyarbakır, Van, Malatya, Denizli and Isparta, pass to the administration of the Grand National Assembly government.

OLAYLAR_EK7:1406-10-15:0.d: After returning from exile following Timur's death in 1405, the Qaraquyunlu ruler Qara Yusuf took Avnik and regained his lands in Eastern Anatolia; he then marched against Timur's grandson Abu Bakr Mirza, who was regarded as the master of Azerbaijan and the two Iraqs, and defeated him on the banks of the Aras. This victory did not give Tabriz to the Qaraquyunlu: the TDV entry on Tabriz states that the city was in the hands of Abu Bakr Mirza in 1408; the battle that won Azerbaijan is the battle of Sardrud on 13 April 1408.

OLAYLAR_EK7:1735-03-21:0.d: Russia, seeking an alliance with Iran against the Ottoman threat, returned the Caspian coastal cities it had held for thirteen years to Iran, under the command of Nadir Khan (who had not yet taken the title of shah), by the Treaty of Ganja. According to the TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi entry on Derbent, this withdrawal was a result of Russia's not wanting to struggle on two fronts (Ottoman and Iranian) in the south, and it strengthened the military prestige that paved the way for Nadir's accession to the throne a few years later. Tarki (Tarku), under Russian administration, also returned to the Iranian side with this withdrawal (the Ganja day is used on the map). Salyan and Shabran, under Russian administration, likewise return to the Iranian side with this withdrawal (no settlement-specific day in the source, the Ganja day is used on the map — approximate information).

OLAYLAR_EK8:1924-01-01:0.d: By the Soviet decision of 'national delimitation' (natsionalno-territorialnoe razmezhevanie), the Khwarazm Soviet Socialist Republic and the Bukharan People's Soviet Republic were abolished; their territories were divided between the newly established Uzbek and Turkmen Soviet Socialist Republics (the east of Khiva to Uzbekistan, the west to Turkmenistan). The TDV entry on Khwarazm: 'In 1924 the eastern parts of the Khanate of Khiva were left to the Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic and the western side to the Turkmen Soviet Socialist Republic.' (the entry gives only the year).

OLAYLAR_EK11:1502-01-01:0.d: After defeating Alvand Bey at Sharur and entering Tabriz in the summer of 1501, Shah Ismail advanced northwest the following year and brought under his rule the line stretching from Erzurum to the Lake Van basin. After the death of Uzun Hasan, the Akkoyunlu State had already been split in two by throne struggles: Alvand Bey held Azerbaijan and Diyarbakır, while his cousin Murad held Persian Iraq and Fars. This division eased the Safavid advance; the region changed hands within a year. Erzurum remained in Safavid hands for sixteen years and came under Ottoman rule only after Çaldıran, in 1518-19. In this year (1502), Aşkale and Pasinler (Hasankale), together with the Erzurum region, passed from the Akkoyunlu to the Safavids (the day could not be verified).

OLAYLAR_EK11:1747-06-20:0.d: Nader Shah, who had put an end to Safavid rule and proclaimed his own sultanate in 1736, marched as far as Delhi in his Indian campaign, and fought three wars with the Ottomans before making peace with the 1746 Treaty of Kerden, was killed in his tent by his own guards. Iran then could not be governed by a single hand: for forty-nine years an Afsharid remnant in Khorasan, the Zands in the south, and the rising Qajars in the north shared the country. Thanks to this fragmentation the Ottoman eastern frontier remained quiet for a long time. Nader Shah was killed on 20 June 1747; according to TDV, the Erivan (Revan) Khanate was founded in the same year (1747) (the day could not be verified).

OLAYLAR_EK14:1568-01-01:0.d: The construction of the Selimiye, which Mimar Sinan called "my masterpiece," began in the name of Selim II in 1568 and, lasting six years, was completed in 1574. The western shops of the arasta and the primary school were completed after Selim II's death, in the reign of Murad III, by Davud Agha.

OLAYLAR_EK16:1941-07-09:0.d: In the third week of Barbarossa the Wehrmacht entered Pskov; the city remained under German military administration until 23 July 1944. Source: Pskov city chronology, memorialmuseums.org «Memorials in Pskov» (information taken from a search summary).

OLAYLAR_EK16:1943-08-05:0.d: The capture of the Orel salient, and, together with Belgorod, the firing of the first artillery salute in Moscow.

OLAYLAR_EK16:1341-01-01:0.d: Uzbek (Özbek/Jani Beg), Khan of the Golden Horde, granted the Principality of Nizhny Novgorod-Gorodets to the Suzdal prince Konstantin Vasilyevich; the principality became a rival of Moscow and was annexed to Moscow by Vasily I in 1392.

OLAYLAR_EK16:1945-05-08:0.b: The Courland Pocket surrendered — the Courland Army Group signed the capitulation to Govorov

OLAYLAR_EK16:1307-01-01:0.d: Polotsk, Vitebsk and their surroundings remained within the Rus' princely dynasty until 1307; the eastward expansion of pre-Gediminas Lithuania became evident with this transition (1307 is taken as the basis here; the actual transfer of Vitebsk, c. 1320, is disputed).

OLAYLAR_EK17:1725-01-01:0.d: During the grand vizierate of Damad Ibrahim Pasha, a committee of thirty-two scholars and scribes, 'which can be regarded as the academy of the age' in the TDV's phrase, was established in Istanbul. The committee brought works of history, philosophy and geography from Arabic, Persian, Greek and Latin into Turkish — among these were Yanyalı Esad Efendi's translation of Aristotle's Physics with a team of twenty-five, and the poet Nedim's presiding over a committee translating a history. The TDV does not specify the day; only the year is known.

OLAYLAR_EK17:1738-08-01:0.d: According to the TDV article on Semendire, the fortress, ceded to Austria at Passarowitz in 1717, was recaptured through the Ottoman advance on the Danube-Sava front of the Ottoman-Austrian War that began in 1737; Habsburg (crown of the Kingdom of Hungary) forces were able to hold on in the region until August 1738, after which date Semendire came under Ottoman administration again. The Treaty of Belgrade (18 September 1739), signed a year later, would confirm this gain — together with Belgrade and northern Serbia.

OLAYLAR_EK17:1738-08-01:1.d: With the recapture of Semendire in August 1738, the Morava valley lying between Semendire and the main body of the Ottoman Empire also returned to Ottoman administration: Jagodina, Kragujevac and Čačak are counted as Ottoman from this date. The sources do not date and mention the return of these three places separately; on the map the date of Semendire has been taken as the basis. The Treaty of Belgrade (18 September 1739) confirmed this situation.

OLAYLAR_EK17:1800-04-02:0.d: In 1799 the combined Russo-Ottoman fleet had expelled the French from the Ionian Islands (the fortress of Corfu fell on 5 March 1799); by a twelve-article convention dated 21 March 1800 the islands were constituted as the Cezâyir-i Seb'a-i Müctemia Cumhuru (Republic of the Seven Islands), autonomous in internal affairs and dependent on the Ottoman Empire in external affairs. The period between 5 March 1799 and this day is one of joint occupation.

OLAYLAR_EK20:1490-01-01:0.d: The united Kingdom of Georgia, ruled by the Bagratid dynasty, was formally divided into three kingdoms after a long internal struggle: Kartli, centered on Tiflis, in the east; Kakheti in the northeast; and Imereti, with its center at Kutaisi, in the west. The TDV article on Georgia confirms the division — 'Georgia was divided into three kingdoms (Kartli, Kakheti, Imereti) and five principalities'. The division was decisive in the Ottoman-Safavid rivalry of the following century: according to the 1555 Treaty of Amasya, Imereti, Dadiani, Guria and Daveli were left to the Ottomans; Kartli, Kakheti and Mosuk to the Safavids. That is, the fact that on the map western and eastern Georgia appear attached to different masters arises from this division. Selim the Grim, while still governor of Trabzon, had in 1508 subjected the Kingdom of Imereti (Açıkbaş) to obedience and tribute.

OLAYLAR_EK20:1768-05-15:0.d: The Republic of Genoa ceded to France Corsica, which it had held for centuries but could no longer effectively control because of revolts. The TDV entry on Corsica gives the event in a single sentence: Genoa, unable to hold on to this island, sold it to France in 1768. The transfer marks Genoa's withdrawal from its last major territorial holding in the Mediterranean; the island will pass to the British for a time in 1796 and then be returned to France. That the island was French territory made Napoleon Bonaparte, born in Ajaccio a year later, a French subject. In this year (1768) Corsica, including Bastia, was sold by Genoa to France (TDV Korsika; the day could not be verified).

OLAYLAR_EK20:1870-09-20:0.d: When the overthrow of Napoleon III in the Franco-Prussian War led to the withdrawal of the French garrison protecting Rome, Italian troops entered the city and the pope retreated to the Vatican. Thus the Papal States, which had existed for more than a thousand years, came to an end, and the Kingdom of Italy, which also added Rome to the union, came onto the European and world stage as a political power. This is an event with direct consequences for the following half century: united Italy is the state that would take Tripolitania and the Dodecanese from the Ottomans in 1911.

OLAYLAR_EK20:1807-07-09:0.d: After the Jena-Auerstedt rout, Prussia had to accept a heavy peace with Napoleon at Tilsit (9 July 1807). It gave up all its lands west of the Elbe and the Polish lands it had received in the 1793 and 1795 partitions; from the latter the Duchy of Warsaw was founded and the area around Białystok was given to Russia. Prussia lost about half its population and territory, and its army was limited to 42,000. On the map, Poznań and Toruń pass to the Duchy of Warsaw from this day, and Białystok to Russia. By this treaty Łódź and Częstochowa (Polish provinces that passed to Prussia after 1772) passed to the Duchy of Warsaw; Gdańsk (Danzig) became an independent free city.

OLAYLAR_EK22:1923-07-24:0.d:
Sèvres (10 August 1920) was a document imposed on the Istanbul government and never entered into force; Lausanne (24 July 1923), by contrast, is the peace that Ankara signed as an equal party and that the Grand National Assembly of Turkey ratified on 23 August 1923 (Lausanne art. 1, 143). On borders, Sèvres pulls Turkey's European frontier back to the Çatalca line and gives Eastern Thrace including Edirne, together with Imbros and Tenedos, to Greece (Sèvres art. 27, 84); İzmir and its surroundings remain Turkish in name only while administration is left to Greece, and after five years a local parliament may request annexation (art. 65-83). Lausanne draws the Maritsa-Arda line, Edirne and Karaağaç remain in Turkey, and Imbros and Tenedos become Turkish (Lausanne art. 2, 12, 14; Karaağaç Protocol). On the Straits, Sèvres establishes an international commission extending over all the waters, on which the Turkish member has only one vote; fortifications are razed and the zone is opened to Allied use (Sèvres art. 36-61, 178-180). Lausanne preserves the principle of free passage but leaves a commission with a Turkish chairman, demilitarized zones and a 12,000-man garrison in Istanbul (Lausanne art. 23; Straits Convention). The recognition of Armenia and the arbitration of the border by the US president, as well as the Kurdish autonomy plan (Sèvres art. 62-64, 88-93), do not appear in Lausanne. Regarding the Arab lands, Egypt, Sudan and Cyprus, Sèvres lays down detailed transfer provisions (Sèvres art. 94-97 mandates, art. 98-100 Hejaz, art. 101-122 renunciation of Egypt, Sudan, Cyprus, Morocco, Tunisia and Libya; the TDV's article ranges are the same); Lausanne words the renunciation more briefly, the Dodecanese go to Italy and Cyprus to Britain, and the Mosul border is postponed (Lausanne art. 3, 15-21). Sèvres re-establishes and extends the capitulations, supervises the Turkish budget and borrowing through a Financial Commission, caps the armed force (gendarmerie and reinforcement elements) at 50,000 men, and prohibits military and naval aviation (Sèvres art. 155, 164, 191-195, 231-264, 261-263). Lausanne abolishes the capitulations, apportions the debts and imposes no separate army limit (Lausanne art. 28, 46-63; art. 113 also abolishes foreign post offices). Minority provisions are broader and open to Allied intervention in Sèvres, whereas in Lausanne they are guaranteed by the League of Nations and reciprocal (Sèvres art. 140-151; Lausanne art. 37-45).

Axis-by-axis comparison:
• Eastern Thrace, Edirne, Çatalca — Sèvres: the Çatalca line is the border; Eastern Thrace and Edirne to Greece (art. 27, 84-85) | Lausanne: border along the Maritsa and Arda; Edirne and Karaağaç remain in Turkey (art. 2; Karaağaç Protocol)
• İzmir region — Sèvres: sovereignty Turkish, administration and army Greek, annexation request after five years (art. 65-83) | Lausanne: no special-status article for İzmir; Anatolia lies within Turkey's borders (art. 2-3 general border; no article specific to İzmir can be cited)
• Straits and Istanbul — Sèvres: International Straits Commission, Turkey 1 vote; razing of fortifications, zone under Allied use; Istanbul in Turkish hands but subject to a minority condition (art. 36-61, 178-180) | Lausanne: principle of free passage; commission with a Turkish chairman, demilitarized zones, 12,000-man garrison in Istanbul (art. 23; Straits Convention)
• Armenia and Kurdistan — Sèvres: Armenia recognized, its border determined by the US president; Kurdish autonomy, independence application after one year (art. 62-64, 88-93) | Lausanne: no relevant provision (not mentioned in the summaries of articles 1-143)
• Aegean islands, Dodecanese — Sèvres: Imbros, Tenedos and the Aegean islands to Greece; Dodecanese and Kastellorizo to Italy (art. 84, 122) | Lausanne: Imbros and Tenedos in Turkey, Eastern Aegean islands Greek, Dodecanese and Kastellorizo in Italy (art. 12-15)
• Cyprus, Egypt, Sudan, Arab lands — Sèvres: mandates over Syria/Mesopotamia and Palestine, Hejaz independent; Egyptian protectorate, Sudan and the annexation of Cyprus recognized (art. 94-98, 101-117) | Lausanne: Syrian border left to the 1921 Franco-Turkish agreement, Iraqi border to later; renunciation of Egypt, Sudan, Cyprus (art. 3, 16-20)
• Capitulations — Sèvres: re-established and extended; judicial reform plan in an Allied commission (art. 136, 261-263, 308-309) | Lausanne: abolished entirely; foreign post offices and the High Health Council abolished (art. 28, 113-114)
• Financial control and debts — Sèvres: Allied Financial Commission supervises budget and borrowing, the Ottoman Public Debt expands, revenues pledged as security (art. 231-264) | Lausanne: Ottoman Public Debt divided among the states; war damages mutually waived (art. 46-63, 58)
• Military restrictions — Sèvres: army of 50,000, air force and tanks prohibited, Allied Control Commissions (art. 152-207) | Lausanne: no general restriction; demilitarization only on the Greek islands and in the Straits and Thrace regions (art. 13; Straits and Thrace conventions)
• Minorities — Sèvres: Allied guarantee and right of intervention, annulment of the Abandoned Properties law, restitution (art. 140-151, 86, 142-144) | Lausanne: rights guaranteed by the League of Nations for non-Muslim minorities, reciprocal Muslim rights in Greece; Greek-Turkish population exchange (art. 37-45; Exchange Convention)
• Legal status — Sèvres: signed by the Istanbul government, rejected by Ankara, never entered into force (TDV) | Lausanne: equal party; ratification by the Grand National Assembly on 2 August 1923, 213 votes for, 14 against (TDV; art. 1, 143)

OLAYLAR_SENKRON_0930:1436-01-01:0.d: The Mamluk army defeated the Dulkadirids at Antep in 1436, and Mehmed Bey withdrew to Akdağ. The year of Besni's return to the Mamluks is not written in the source; Besni had been joined to Dulkadir in 1418, and had returned to the Mamluks before Shahsuvar Bey took it from them in 1465. On the map, Besni returns to the Mamluks together with this defeat at the neighbouring center of Antep (approximate information).

OLAYLAR_2S0920:1941-05-05:0.d: After British-Ethiopian forces took Addis Ababa in early April, Emperor Haile Selassie returned triumphantly to the capital on 5 May 1941; this day is counted as the official end of the Italian occupation (1936-41).

OLAYLAR_2S0920:1942-01-01:0.d: During the Borneo campaign, a small Japanese force landed on the undefended island of Labuan and seized it; the island remained under Japanese military occupation from January 1942 to September 1945. The day varies in the sources as 1 or 3 January.

OLAYLAR_2S0920:0224-04-28:0.d: In Fars, the local ruler Ardashir defeated the Parthian ruler Artabanus V at Hormozgan; the Parthian (Arsacid) dynasty collapsed and the Sasanian dynasty rose. On the map, Isfahan is regarded as Sasanian land from this day.

OLAYLAR_SENUSI_0919:1691-01-01:0.d: The sancak of Lugos remained under Habsburg (German) occupation between 1691 and 1695; Mustafa II reconquered it on 22 September 1695. On the map it is shown as Habsburg between 1691 and 1695, and the period 1689–1691 remains blank. The date has been taken as a year only.

OLAYLAR_SENUSI_0919:1716-10-18:0.d: Lugoj, a sanjak fortress dependent on the Eyalet of Temesvár, had been in Ottoman hands since 1695; with the surrender of the provincial center at the end of the 1716 siege, it was left to the Habsburg Monarchy.

OLAYLAR_SENUSI_0919:1688-01-01:0.d: In the campaign of 1688, after taking Karánsebes, General Veterani marched on Orsova and occupied it as well. The source gives no day for the occupation; since only the year is known, 1 January 1688 has been used.

OLAYLAR_SENUSI_0919:1717-01-01:0.d: In the campaign of 1717, General Splényi arrived before Orsova on 27 August and took the town easily; Orsova, which Mercy had been unable to take in 1716, thus passed into Habsburg hands. Because on the map the surrounding Danube-bank areas (including the Đerdap section on the Serbian side) depend on Orsova, the nearest settlement, they are shown as belonging to the same owner as it. The date has been taken as a year only; the exact day could not be verified.

OLAYLAR_SERHAT:1428-01-01:0.d: After the childless death of the Serbian Despot Stefan Lazarević (1427), Murad II, claiming to be the legitimate heir of Serbia on the basis of Bayezid the Thunderbolt's marriage to a Serbian princess, took action and took Alacahisar (1428). In the same year, after Lazarević's death, the Ottomans also recovered the fortress of Şehirköy — the town had been taken by Stefan in 1412 and defended against Musa Çelebi. According to the TDV article on Niš, the Ottomans retook Niš in the same year as well (831/1428). Thus the line connecting the Great Morava and Nišava valleys came under Ottoman control.

OLAYLAR_P0049:1724-05-06:0.d: During the Iranian campaign begun in 1723, Khoy together with Kapan and the Karadağ region passed again to Ottoman administration on 6 May 1724 and was recorded in the Ottoman survey in 1728. The map also shows Kotur, 40 km southwest of Khoy, as having passed from the Safavids to the Ottomans on this day (the date of Khoy was taken as the basis: Uluerler 2015, Turkish Studies 10/5, p. 6; no day specific to Kotur in the source — approximate information).

OLAYLAR_P0057:1921-04-07:0.d: After the Greek offensive that was halted on 1 April at the Second İnönü, Afyon was retaken on 7 April on the southern front. The TDV article on the National Struggle summarizes this as 'after a heavy defeat at Aslıhanlar, Afyon was retaken on 7 April'; however, military-history studies place the Aslıhanlar–Dumlupınar fighting after the evacuation of Afyon, between 8 and 15 April, and write that tactical superiority remained on the Greek side — the two accounts do not agree. The victory of İnönü was celebrated with rallies throughout the country, first of all in Istanbul.

OLAYLAR_P0057:1921-01-01:0.b: The end of the Italian occupation of Burdur

OLAYLAR_ARKEOLOJI_ZINCIR:-0309-01-01:0.d: Alexander IV (323-310 BC), the last king of the Argead kingship, was killed together with his mother Roxane; the Empire of Alexander entry ends with this year. The later owner of Pasargadae and Susa has not been sourced. Babylon, Uruk and Hamadan pass to Seleucus before this date.

OLAYLAR_ARKEOLOJI_ZINCIR:0009-01-10:0.d: Wang Mang received the will in the golden casket at the Han's High Temple, ascended the throne and named the dynasty Xin; the Western Han ended. Because the source does not record Xin-period ownership for Dunhuang and Zhangye in the Hexi corridor, the map shows these places as blank. Chang'an passed directly to Xin.

OLAYLAR_ARKEOLOJI_ZINCIR:0025-01-01:0.d: At Chengdu, ownership passes from the ownerless interval to Chengjia (成家, Gongsun Shu). Transition source information: Hou Han shu 13 (Gongsun Shu): in the Gengshi period he became 'King of Shu' and made Chengdu his capital; in Jianwu 1 (25 CE), 4th month, he proclaimed himself emperor; its end in Jianwu 12 (Wu Han's campaign, siege of Chengdu).

OLAYLAR_ARKEOLOJI_ZINCIR:0027-01-01:0.d: Xi'an (Chang'an) appears blank on the map after the period of the Red Eyebrows Regime (Jianshi). Source: Hou Han shu 1a, Jianwu 1: Chimei entered Chang'an and burned the palace; in the same month Deng Yu entered Chang'an and carried the tablets of the 11 emperors to Gao Miao (a brief Han entry). Chimei's departure from Chang'an (the end of the entry, AD 27) has not yet been verified from the source.

OLAYLAR_ARKEOLOJI_ZINCIR:0036-01-01:0.d: At Chengdu, ownership passes from Chengjia (成家, Gongsun Shu) to the ownerless interval. Transition source information: Sanguozhi 32 (Xianzhu zhuan): Liu Bei besieged Chengdu for tens of days and Liu Zhang surrendered (under the heading Jian'an 19 = 214); in Zhangwu 1 (221) he became emperor. End: Sanguozhi 28 (Deng Ai): Liu Shan sent the imperial seal and surrendered, Ai entered Chengdu, and Liu Shan came out with the prince and notables.

OLAYLAR_ARKEOLOJI_ZINCIR:0221-01-01:0.d: At Chengdu, ownership passes from the ownerless interval to Shu Han. Transition source information: Sanguozhi 32 (Xianzhu zhuan): Liu Bei besieged Chengdu for tens of days and Liu Zhang surrendered (under the heading Jian'an 19 = 214); in Zhangwu 1 (221) he became emperor. End: Sanguozhi 28 (Deng Ai): Liu Shan sent the imperial seal and surrendered, Ai entered Chengdu, and Liu Shan came out with the prince and notables.

OLAYLAR_ARKEOLOJI_ZINCIR:0395-01-01:0.d: At Rome, ownership passes from the Roman Empire (Principate-Dominate, combined) to the ownerless interval. Transition source information: Marcellinus Comes, Chronicon s.a. 476 (consulship of Basiliscus and Armatus; Mommsen CM II, Latin Library marcellinus1.html): Odoacer took Rome, killed Orestes, exiled Augustulus to Lucullanum, and the Western empire perished with Augustulus.

OLAYLAR_ARKEOLOJI_D2_IRAN_ORTA_ASYA:-319.d: The undeciphered Proto-Elamite writing system at Susa, contemporary with Uruk III; it spreads to eight sites on the Iranian plateau. Sources give a beginning of 3200.

OLAYLAR_ARKEOLOJI_D2_AFRIKA_AMERIKA:-374.d: The oldest known adobe monumental structure on the northern Peruvian coast (Chao Valley); the study dates the 'invention of adobe architecture before 5,100 calendar years B.P.' It is linked to El Niño rains.

OLAYLAR_ARKEOLOJI_MISIR_NIL_SAHRA:-1069-.d: The Napata-centered period of the Kushite dynasty; the center shifts to Meroe in ~300 BCE. The 25th Dynasty (Kush), which conquered Egypt, falls in this period — this source does not include the dates of the 25th Dynasty.

OLAYLAR_T5_1000A:1008-01-01:0.d: The source shows the city of Batumi under the administration of the Kingdom/Kingdoms of Georgia at this date; earlier ownership is not dated in the source (the map shows the period before this date as blank).

OLAYLAR_T5_1000A:1096-01-01:0.d: The Seljuk emir Kerbogha took Mosul from the Uqaylids. (Dhu'l-Qa'da 489 / November 1096; here only the year has been taken as the basis.)

OLAYLAR_T5_1000A:1100-01-01:0.d: The source shows the city of Niksar under the administration of the Danishmendids at this date; earlier ownership is not dated in the source (the map shows the period before this date as blank).

OLAYLAR_T5_1000A:1116-01-01:0.d: The source shows the city of Niğde under the administration of the Anatolian (Turkey) Seljuk State at this date; earlier ownership is not dated in the source (the map shows the period before this date as blank).

OLAYLAR_T5_1000A:1119-01-01:0.d: The Byzantine emperor John II Komnenos forced the Seljuk commander in Laodicea, Alp Kara, to withdraw; the lands of Denizli passed to Byzantium again (the Byzantine entry gives the date 1120).

OLAYLAR_T5_1000A:1134-01-01:0.d: The source shows the city of Kayseri under the administration of the Danishmendids at this date; earlier ownership is not dated in the source (the map shows the period before this date as blank).

OLAYLAR_T5_1000A:1142-01-01:0.d: The source shows the city of Kemah under the administration of the Mengujekids (Mengücekoğulları) at this date; earlier ownership is not dated in the source (the map shows the period before this date as blank).

OLAYLAR_T5_1000A:1148-01-01:0.d: With the dissolution of the Seljuks, Nakhchivan joined the State of the Ildegizids and was their centre until 1174 (the year of joining is not specified; the beginning of the dynasty has been taken as the basis).

OLAYLAR_T5_1000A:1160-01-01:0.d: The source shows the city of Baku under the administration of the Shirvanshahs at this date; earlier ownership is not dated in the source (the map shows the period before this date as blank).

OLAYLAR_T5_1000A:1199-01-06:0.d: The Rubenid dynasty, which held Adana and Tarsus, took the title of kingdom; this is a change of title of the same dynasty, and no territory changed hands. The coronation day was NOT FOUND in TDV — the date used here for the beginning of the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia has been taken as the basis (this date does not rest on a source).

OLAYLAR_T5_1000A:1204-04-13:0.d: The source shows the city of Kütahya under the administration of the Empire of Nicaea (Laskaris) at this date; earlier ownership is not dated in the source (the map shows the period before this date as blank).

OLAYLAR_T5_1000A:1211-01-01:0.d: The source shows the city of Kastamonu under the administration of the Çobanoğulları at this date; earlier ownership is not dated in the source (the map shows the period before this date as blank).

OLAYLAR_T5_1000A:1225-01-01:0.d: Jalāl al-Dīn Khwarazmshah added Azerbaijan and Arran to his lands (the information in the source concerns the region as a whole).

OLAYLAR_T5_1000A:1231-01-01:1.d: With the collapse of Jalāl al-Dīn Khwarazmshah, Tabriz suffered the Mongol occupation in 1231; in the same year Mongol rule covered Northern and Southern Azerbaijan (this information concerns the region as a whole, it is not specific to the city). In Shirvan (Baku, Shamakhi) the Shirvanshahs continued to exist as a local dynasty under Mongol sovereignty; on the map these two places are shown in the Shirvanshah colour (there was Mongol/Ilkhanid vassalage).

OLAYLAR_T5_1000A:1233-01-01:1.d: With the death of the last Zengid atabeg, Badr al-Dīn Luʾluʾ was proclaimed sultan by the caliph. (Rabīʿ al-awwal 631 / December 1233; here only the year has been taken as the basis.)

OLAYLAR_T5_1000A:1256-01-01:0.d: With Hülegü's arrival in Iran, Mongol administration passed to the Ilkhanid State; Qazvin and Nakhchivan passed to Ilkhanid administration (the date used is not a day given in the source). In Shirvan (Baku, Shamakhi) the Mongol occupation brought heavy destruction, but the Shirvanshahs continued as a local dynasty; on the map these two places are shown in the Shirvanshah colour.

OLAYLAR_T5_1000B:1171-09-13:0.d: With Saladin's vizierate and the death of the Fatimid caliph al-ʿĀḍid (567/1171), Egypt passed to the Ayyubids; Alexandria and the Fayyum came under Ayyubid administration. The day is not in the source — the end day used for the Fatimids has been taken as the basis (this day does not rest on a source). The Hejaz also came under Ayyubid administration; the suzerainty of Mecca passed from the Fatimids to the Ayyubids.

OLAYLAR_T5_1000B:1250-04-30:0.d: After Turanshah, Mamluk power was established with Shajar al-Durr and ʿIzz al-Dīn Aybak; the Egyptian cities (Alexandria, Mansura, the Fayyum) passed to Mamluk administration. The source gives Aybak's accession as 3 July 1250; here the end day used for the Ayyubids (30 April 1250) has been taken as the basis; this day does not rest on a source, and there is a difference between the two dates.

OLAYLAR_T5_1000B:1261-07-25:0.d: Nicaean troops entered Constantinople on 25 July 1261, ending Latin rule; the lands of the Laskaris (Nicaea) state — Bursa, İzmir, Çimpe, Adrianople, Thessalonica — became the Byzantine Empire again. At these points the map shows the period of the Empire of Nicaea before 1261 only at the places that are named in the source.

OLAYLAR_ONCE1000_1019:0990-03-31:0.d: The Uqaylid Abū'l-Zawwād Muhammad b. al-Musayyab seized Mosul (380 / 990); 31 March 990, the first day of the period in which Hijri year 380 and the year 990 overlap, was taken as the basis (Hijri-Gregorian table, ±1-2 days); the day is not in the source.

OLAYLAR_KURULUS_GERI_1021:0762-01-01:0.d: Construction work on the city founded on the bank of the Tigris began in 762; it became the permanent capital of the Abbasids (only its year is known).

OLAYLAR_KURULUS_GERI_1021:0945-12-19:0.d: Ahmad entered Baghdad on 11 Jumādā I 334 (19 December 945); the caliph al-Mustakfī made him amīr al-umarāʾ, and the city passed to the rule of the Buyids (Kufa also came under Buyid rule (945-1055); for Kufa the day of neighbouring Baghdad was taken as the basis).

OLAYLAR_KURULUS_GERI_1021:0745-01-01:0.d: With the rebellion of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Ḥabīb in 745, Kairouan left the Umayyad governorship; a Habibid/Kharijite interim until 761 (its owner is uncertain; the map shows this period as blank).

OLAYLAR_KURULUS_GERI_1021:0972-10-02:0.d: In the name of the Fatimid caliph, Buluggīn b. Zīrī governed Ifriqiya; the Zirids (972-1057) ruled Kairouan (TDV gives only the year; the day used does not rest on this source).

OLAYLAR_KURULUS_GERI_1021:1057-01-01:0.d: Around 449 (1057) the Hilalis plundered Kairouan; the Zirids withdrew to Mahdia; the owner of the city until 1229 cannot be traced year by year in the sources (the map shows this period as blank).

OLAYLAR_KURULUS_GERI_1021:0750-08-05:0.d: The last Umayyad caliph, Marwān II, was killed on 26 Dhū'l-Ḥijja 132 / 5 August 750; Mecca entered the Abbasid governorship of the Haramayn (no day specific to Mecca — the day the state ended was taken as the basis; approximate information).

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_ORTADOGU:0754-01-01:0.b: Al-Manṣūr became caliph (754-775); the period regarded as that of the true founder of the caliphate began.
OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_ORTADOGU:0754-01-01:0.d: Al-Manṣūr became caliph (754-775); the period regarded as that of the true founder of the caliphate began.

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_ORTADOGU:0820-06-17:0.d: Hamdawayh b. Mahan, who had declared independence, was eliminated by Isa b. Yazid al-Jaludi (205/820); Sana'a and its surroundings were governed by Abbasid governors sent from Baghdad until the year 232 (847). With this date the gap at Sana'a on the map (815-820) ends and the Abbasid Caliphate period begins.

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_ORTADOGU:0870-08-29:0.d: The fleet under the command of Ahmad b. Umar, one of the Aghlabid commanders in Sicily, definitively seized Malta (28 Ramadan 256 / 29 August 870); the island had been under Byzantine (Eastern Roman) rule since 533, and after this date Muslim rule became permanent.

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_ORTADOGU:0929-02-14:0.d: The Ismaili Qarmatians (Qarmatian State of Bahrain) occupied Mecca in 317 AH / 929 and carried the Black Stone to al-Ahsā' (Lahsā'); it was put back in its place twenty years later.

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_ORTADOGU:1076-08-05:0.d: Abdallah b. Ali al-Uyuni, of the Banu Murra branch of the Abd al-Qays tribe, seized Lahsa at the end of a siege lasting seven years (469/1076); with this event the rule of the Qarmatian State of Bahrain in Lahsa came to an end. On the map Lahsa is shown as blank after this date (the Uyunids are not shown separately).

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_ORTADOGU:1102-05-22:0.d: The Qarakhanid Harun Tegin, who wanted to seize Khorasan by exploiting the confusion among Malik-Shah's sons and had captured Tirmidh, was taken prisoner by the Seljuk Sultan Sanjar and executed (2 Sha'ban 495 / 22 May 1102). On the map, Tirmidh (Termez) is shown as belonging to the Great Seljuk State from this day; this is an inference from the event (approximate information).

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_ORTADOGU:1236-01-01:0.b: Al-Aziz Muhammad died; his seven-year-old son al-Nasir Yusuf II became ruler of Aleppo (Rabi' al-Awwal 634 / November 1236; the day is unknown).
OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_ORTADOGU:1236-01-01:0.d: Al-Aziz Muhammad died; his seven-year-old son al-Nasir Yusuf II became ruler of Aleppo (Rabi' al-Awwal 634 / November 1236; the day is unknown).

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_IRAN_TURAN:1092-11-19:0.d: About a month after Nizam al-Mulk was killed by the Batinis, Malikshah died in Baghdad (16 Shawwal 485 / 19 November 1092); the state stretched from Kashgar to the Aegean islands and from the Aral Sea and the Caucasus to Yemen and Aden, and the Karakhanids too were subject to the empire. After his death a struggle for the sultanate began among the members of the dynasty: the eldest son Berkyaruq was proclaimed sultan in Rayy by the ghulams attached to Nizam al-Mulk (485/1092; the day is not specified in TDV, after Malikshah's death), and a struggle began with Terken Khatun and the Turkish emirs, who wished to place her young son Mahmud on the throne.

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_IRAN_TURAN:1101-11-16:0.b: Arslan-Shah I (son of Kirmanshah) ascended the throne of Kirman; Iranshah had been killed by fatwa and popular uprising

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_IRAN_TURAN:1219-01-01:0.d: Toward the end of 1219 the Mongol armies entered the lands of the Khwarazm-Shahs; the fortified places of Transoxiana fell one by one, and the places that resisted were subjected to massacre (such as Otrar, Sighnaq and Khujand). On the map, Khujand is shown under Mongol ownership from 1219.

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_IBERYA_MAGRIB:1002-01-01.b: The hajib Mansur b. Abi Amir died at Medinaceli after his 52nd campaign against Castile (392/1002; the source gives only the year).
OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_IBERYA_MAGRIB:1002-01-01.d: The hajib Mansur b. Abi Amir died at Medinaceli after his 52nd campaign against Castile (392/1002; the source gives only the year).

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_IBERYA_MAGRIB:1085-05-08.d: At the end of a siege lasting about nine months, Toledo was surrendered peacefully to the Kingdom of Castile of Alfonso VI (8 May 1085); the Dhu'l-Nunid ruler Yahya al-Qadir went to Valencia with his family and retinue and reigned there. On the map, from this day Valencia is shown as the Muluk al-Tawa'if (Andalusian taifa emirates) instead of the Dhu'l-Nunids (Taifa of Toledo).

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_BIZANS_BALKAN:1207-01-01.d: Marco Sanudo, nephew of the Venetian Doge Dandolo, landed in the Aegean islands with an adventurous band; seventeen islands surrendered easily, only Naxos resisted, and the duchy founded there in 1207 lasted more than three centuries. Sanudo himself offered his allegiance not to Venice but to the Latin Emperor Henry.

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_BATI_AVRUPA:0858-02-13:0.d: According to the Chronicle of the Kings of Alba, the historical list of the kings of Alba (Scotland), Cináed mac Ailpín died at the palace of Forteviot on 13 February; the Annals of Ulster place his death in 858.

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_ITALYA_DOGU_AVRUPA:0966-.d: Mieszko I, the first historical ruler of the Piast dynasty, accepted Christianity according to the Latin rite in 966 (according to TDV, from 967); the first bishopric was founded at Posen (Poznań) in 968 at the latest.

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_ITALYA_DOGU_AVRUPA:0980-.b: Vladimir takes Kiev and has Yaropolk killed; he becomes Grand Prince of Kiev

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_ITALYA_DOGU_AVRUPA:1000-.d: On the proposal of the lawspeaker Þorgeir Ljósvetningagoði, 'one law, one religion', the Althing adopted Christianity as the official religion (only the year is known). The SNL, in 'Islands historie', also confirms this: 'I 981 kom ... de første misjonærene til øya, og i 999/1000 fikk utsendinger fra Olav Tryggvason vedtatt kristendommen på Alltinget.'

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_ITALYA_DOGU_AVRUPA:1056-.d: Ísleifur Gissurarson was consecrated by the Archbishop of Bremen as the first bishop of Iceland; Skálholt became the episcopal seat (only the year is known).

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_ITALYA_DOGU_AVRUPA:1096-.d: Through the efforts of Bishop Gissur Ísleifsson, the Althing adopted the church tithe, Iceland's first real tax (the Althings of 1096-97; only the year is known). SNL 'Islands historie': 'Under hans sønn Gissur ble tiende innført, og det ble også opprettet et bispesete på Hólar'.

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_ITALYA_DOGU_AVRUPA:1115-.d: The House of Canossa (Canossa/Matilda) came to an end. According to Treccani's entry 'Matilde di Canossa', Matilda's estate comprised Brescia, Bergamo, Mantua and the counties of Arezzo, Siena and Corneto.

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_ITALYA_DOGU_AVRUPA:1150-.d: King Eric IX (1150-1160) organised the Swedish church on the Western model and, by conducting a crusade against the pagan Finns, began Sweden's overseas rule. (The year of the expedition is not given in the source.)

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_ITALYA_DOGU_AVRUPA:1241-.d: The Mongols destroyed Halych; Danylo moved the capital to Kholm (its day is unknown; only the year has been taken as the basis). Encyclopedia of Ukraine ('Galicia-Volhynia'): 'After the Mongols razed Halych in 1241, Kholm became the new capital.'

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_ANADOLU_KAFKASYA:1260-01.d: When the Ilkhanid Mongols were defeated by the Mamluks and withdrew to Iran, the Mamluks attacked Cilicia and devastated the country; this is the actual beginning of the Mamluk attacks.

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_IRAN_HINT_MAGRIB:1062-01.b: Tughril Beg campaigned against Tarum and imposed a heavy tribute on Malik Musafir
OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_IRAN_HINT_MAGRIB:1062-01.d: Tughril Beg campaigned against Tarum and imposed a heavy tribute on Malik Musafir

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_BOZKIR:0895-03-02:0.d: The Pechenegs, allied with the Bulgarian King Simeon, attacked the Magyars and forced them to migrate to Pannonia (282/895); they brought under their rule the steppe region stretching from the Don river to the Danube river.

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_CIN:0640-10-11:0.b: The An-Xi Protectorate was established at Xizhou
OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_CIN:0640-10-11:0.d: After the annexation of Gaochang, serious crimes were pardoned in the new prefecture of Xizhou (9th month, 癸卯) and the An-Xi Protectorate (Anxi duhufu) was established at Xizhou.

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_CIN:0821-01-01:0.b: The Tang-Tibetan treaty was sworn at Chang'an (821)

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_CIN:1129-08-01:0.b: Hangzhou was raised to 'Lin'an Prefecture' (Lin'an fu)
OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_CIN:1129-08-01:0.d: Gaozong's court raised Hangzhou to the status of Lin'an Prefecture (Lin'an fu).

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_DOGU_GUNEYDOGU_ASYA:0929.d: Judging by the locations where the inscriptions are found, Coedès writes that the administrative center of the kingdom moved eastward during the reign of Wawa (927-928) and that Rakai Halu Sindok, named in the inscription of 919, took the throne ten years later, in 929. Thus the center of Medang shifted to the Brantas basin (East Java).

OLAYLAR_ORTACAG_DOGU_GUNEYDOGU_ASYA:0936.d: At the call of Gyeon Hwon, the founder of Hubaekje, Taejo assembled at Cheonan in the autumn of 936 and advanced to Ilsan-gun; with the appearance of a 'cloud-like sword' before Ilicheon and the surrender of the Hubaekje generals to Gyeon Hwon, the enemy was routed, 3,200 prisoners were taken and 5,700 were killed; Sin-geom and his brothers surrendered. Taejo entered the Hubaekje capital, ordered that the people not be touched, and thus united the three Han.
